articles.title: MP3 vs WAV Explained: What Lossy Compression Actually Throws Away (With a Python Example)
articles.excerpt: By Tania Alwan Export a song from almost any audio tool and you get the same question: MP3 or WAV? The usual answer is "WAV is better quality, MP3 is smaller", which is true but not very useful. This…
articles.body: By Tania Alwan Export a song from almost any audio tool and you get the same question: MP3 or WAV? The usual answer is "WAV is better quality, MP3 is smaller", which is true but not very useful. This post explains what is actually inside each file, how MP3 makes audio so much smaller, and ends with a short Python script that shows exactly where the missing data goes. What a WAV file really is WAV is a container format from Microsoft and IBM, built on the RIFF structure. In practice, almost every WAV you meet holds uncompressed PCM audio : a long list of sample values, one per channel, taken at a fixed rate.
articles.author: Tania Alwan

articles.title: Offset vs Cursor Pagination: Why Your API Slows Down on Page 500 (With PostgreSQL and Node.js Code)
articles.excerpt: Most list endpoints start with LIMIT and OFFSET. It's simple, it works on day one, and it gets quietly slower as the table grows. By the time someone (or a crawler) asks for page 500, the database is…
articles.body: Most list endpoints start with LIMIT and OFFSET . It's simple, it works on day one, and it gets quietly slower as the table grows. By the time someone (or a crawler) asks for page 500, the database is reading and throwing away thousands of rows just to return 20. Cursor pagination (also called keyset pagination) fixes this. Here's how both approaches work, where offset breaks down, and how to build a cursor-based endpoint with PostgreSQL and Node.js. How offset pagination works SELECT id , title , created_at FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 9980 ; PostgreSQL can't jump straight to row 9,981. It has to walk the first 10,000 rows in order and discard 9,980 of them.

articles.body: TITLE: 영지식 증명 프라이버시와 규제 준수: 우리는 정말 두 마리 토끼를 다 잡을 수 있을까? 암호화 기술로 얻는 프라이버시와 규제 당국의 감시, 이 두 마리 토끼를 과연 다 잡을 수 있을까? 블록체인 판에서는 사실 새삼스러운 이야기도 아니다. 다만 영지식 증명(ZKPs)이 등장하면서 그 논의의 판도가 지난 몇 년 새 완전히 뒤바뀌었다고 본다. 내가 이 시장을 처음, 그야말로 무법지대 같던 시절부터 지금처럼 제도권에 편입되면서도 여전히 변동성이 큰 상태까지 지켜봐 온 사람으로서 말이다. 오늘도 비트코인 가격이 64,650달러 언저리를 맴도는 걸 보면, 정말 수많은 기술이 서로 양립 불가능해 보이는 간극을 메워주겠다며 등장하는 걸 봤다. 하지만 영지식 증명은 그저 또 하나의 허황된 약속이 아니다. 검증 가능한, 아주 구체적인 해법을 제시한다. 내 생각은 이렇다. 영지식 증명 기술이 제공하는 프라이버시와 규제 준수 사이의 갈등은 본질적으로 양립 불가능한 문제가 아니다. 오히려 아키텍처 설계, 법적 해석, 그리고 솔직히 말해 교육의 영역에서 풀어야 할 숙제라고 본다. 영지식 증명의 핵심 아이디어, 즉 '기저 데이터를 드러내지 않고도 무언가를 증명한다'는 건, 사실 규제 당국이 이상적으로 추구해야 할 목표와 정확히 일치한다. 불필요한 데이터 수집 없이도 확실한 보증을 얻는 것 말이다. 이 주장의 진위는 프라이버시 옹호론자와 규제 준수 책임자 모두를 만족시키는 영지식 증명 기반 시스템이 성공적으로 구현되는지 여부에 달려 있다.

articles.title: What it really costs to put a PDF viewer and editor in a web app (PDF.js vs the commercial SDKs)
articles.excerpt: If you have ever been asked to "just show the PDF in the app", you know how that ticket goes. Viewing takes an afternoon. Then somebody asks for highlights. Then form filling. Then signatures. Then, o…
articles.body: If you have ever been asked to "just show the PDF in the app", you know how that ticket goes. Viewing takes an afternoon. Then somebody asks for highlights. Then form filling. Then signatures. Then, one day, a customer wants to fix a typo in a contract without leaving your product, and you find out that changing the text that is already inside a PDF is a completely different problem from drawing on top of it. We build a PDF SDK ( Kernstra ), so yes, this post is written by a vendor, and you should read it with that in mind. I have tried to make it useful anyway: where PDF.js is the right answer, where the commercial SDKs are ahead of us, and what the commercial ones actually cost, because that last part is surprisingly hard to find out.

articles.title: Choosing a Real Device Farm? 10 Questions to Ask Before You Sign Up
articles.excerpt: At some point every mobile team reaches the same conclusion: "We need to test on real phones, and we're not going to buy fifty of them." So you start looking at real device farms. And pretty quickly t…
articles.body: At some point every mobile team reaches the same conclusion: "We need to test on real phones, and we're not going to buy fifty of them." So you start looking at real device farms. And pretty quickly they all start to sound the same. Thousands of devices. Fast. Secure. Easy to use. Every landing page promises roughly the same thing. The differences only show up once you actually start using one. Maybe the phones you need are always busy. Maybe your automation doesn't run the way you expected. Maybe the logs you need to debug aren't there. So before you sign up for anything, here are the questions I'd ask. They're not about any particular tool. They're about making sure whatever you pick actually fits how your team works. Choosing a real device farm Lots of phones is a good start.
articles.author: Alok Raj

articles.body: Credit: Oliver Cragg / Android Authority TL;DR The Hokkaido emulator for running Switch 2 games on Android now has built-in Banana Native support. This means you can generate and play native ports of Switch 2 titles via the emulator. Switch 2 emulation and ports require an Android device with high-end silicon and plenty of RAM, though. The Nintendo Switch 2 only launched last year, but we’ve recently seen the first emulators arriving on Android, along with native game ports. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision. Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own. Submissions are due March 1, 2027. Every mission requires a power source. articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 just reached a light-day in space, but Voyager 2 won't do the same until 2035, due to speed choices made throughout their 50-year missions.
articles.body: Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer?

NASA On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year, the hackathon drew 59% more registrants and was the 5th year in a row with increased participation. Since 2012, NASA Space Apps Challenge has hosted the two-day event, which has included more than 600,000 people from more than 190 countries.

articles.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
articles.excerpt: The British company Foundational thinks its laser-reflecting tech can help humanity fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.
articles.body: A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors.
